q: Software that is designed to damage or disturb a computer system is called:
x: Malware is any malicious software, such as viruses and worms. Firmware is built into hardware, freeware is free to use and middleware connects software components.

q: The name given to an unwanted bulk email message is:
x: Spam is unsolicited bulk email, usually advertising. Cookies are small files stored by websites, packets carry network data and a cache stores recently used data.

q: A firewall is mainly used to:
o: Control incoming and outgoing network traffic
Increase the free space on the hard disk
Speed up the main processor of the system
Remove dust from inside the computer case
x: A firewall applies rules that allow or block network connections to protect a system. It has no effect on processor speed or disk capacity.

q: Which type of malware replicates itself across a network without needing to attach to a host file?
x: A worm copies itself from computer to computer on its own. A Trojan pretends to be useful software and needs the user to run it, and spyware secretly collects information.

q: Sending fake emails that trick users into giving passwords or bank details is called:
x: Phishing uses messages that look genuine to steal sensitive information. Spooling queues print jobs, booting starts the computer and formatting prepares a disk.

q: Which of the following is the best protection against losing data after a disk failure?
x: A backup is a separate copy of data that can be restored if the original is lost. The other actions have no effect on data safety.

q: A software that checks files for known malicious code and removes it is called:
x: Antivirus programs scan for signatures and suspicious behaviour of malware. A device driver lets the OS talk to hardware and formatters only prepare disks.

q: Which of the following passwords is the strongest?
x: A strong password is long and mixes upper and lower case letters, digits and symbols that are not a dictionary word. The other choices are common and easy to guess.

q: A virus that attaches itself to the boot sector of a disk is called a:
x: A boot sector virus infects the first sector that the computer reads when starting. A macro virus infects documents that contain macros.

q: Which of the following best describes a Trojan horse?
o: A program that appears useful but hides harmful code
A program that repeats itself across a network by itself
A backup copy of an operating system
x: A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software to trick users into running it. The self-copying program described in the second option is a worm.

q: Which of the following is used to protect data during transmission by converting it into unreadable form?
x: Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the key can read it. Compression reduces size and defragmentation reorganises a disk.

q: A Caesar cipher replaces each letter with the letter 3 places later in the alphabet (A becomes D). How is the word BAT encrypted?
x: B+3 = E, A+3 = D, T+3 = W, giving EDW. YXQ shifts each letter 3 places back instead of forward, and CBU shifts by only 1.

q: A message was encrypted with a Caesar cipher that shifts each letter 3 places forward (A becomes D). The ciphertext is KHOOR. What was the original word?
x: To decrypt, shift each letter 3 places back: K-3 = H, H-3 = E, O-3 = L, O-3 = L, R-3 = O, giving HELLO. NKRRU comes from shifting forward again instead of back.

q: In encryption, what is the scrambled, unreadable form of a message called?
x: Encryption turns readable plaintext into ciphertext, and decryption with the key turns it back. Plaintext is the original readable message.

q: In public-key (asymmetric) encryption, Bilal encrypts a message with Sara's public key. Which key can decrypt it?
x: A message locked with someone's public key can be opened only with the matching private key, which only Sara holds. The public key is shared with everyone, so it cannot be what keeps the message secret.

q: A hidden program secretly records every key a user presses so that an attacker can capture passwords. It is called a:
x: A keylogger is spyware that records keystrokes and sends them to the attacker. A firewall is a protection tool that filters network traffic.

q: Malware locks or encrypts a user's files and then demands payment to unlock them. This type of malware is called:
x: Ransomware holds files hostage and demands a ransom. Adware shows unwanted adverts, while freeware and shareware are licence types, not malware.

q: Which login method is two-factor authentication?
o: A password plus a second, different password
A password plus a one-time code sent to the user's phone
A password plus a four-digit PIN
A user name plus a password
x: Two-factor authentication combines two different kinds of proof, such as something you know (password) and something you have (phone). A second password or a PIN is just another thing you know, so it is still one factor.

q: Which of these is a biometric method of checking a user's identity?
x: Biometrics uses a person's body features, such as fingerprints, face or eyes. A password or PIN is something you know, and a smart card is something you have.

q: Attackers flood a university's admission website with so many fake requests that real students cannot open it. This attack is called:
x: A denial-of-service attack overloads a server so that genuine users are refused service. Phishing tricks people into giving away details, which does not take a site offline.

q: What does copyright protect?
o: Brand names and logos of companies
Original creative works such as software, books and music
x: Copyright gives the creator rights over copying and sharing an original work, including software. Brand names and logos are protected as trademarks.

q: A shop buys one licensed copy of a program and installs it on 20 computers, although the licence allows only one. This is:
x: Installing software beyond what the licence allows is software piracy, which breaks copyright. Paying for one copy does not give the right to make 19 more.

q: A company's logo and brand name are legally protected as a:
x: A trademark protects names, logos and symbols that identify a business. A patent protects a new invention.

q: An engineer invents a new type of machine and wants the legal right to stop others making and selling it. What should she obtain?
x: A patent protects an invention and gives the inventor the right to stop others making or selling it for a period. A trademark protects only a brand name or logo.

q: Software that can be used free for a trial period, after which the user is expected to pay to keep using it, is called:
x: Shareware is 'try before you buy' software. Freeware is free to use with no payment expected at any time.

q: What is special about open-source software?
o: It can be used only for a short trial period
It is always written by a government
Its source code is available to study, change and share under its licence
It has no licence and no conditions at all
x: Open-source software makes its source code available and its licence allows people to modify and share it. A trial period describes shareware, and open-source software still comes with a licence.

q: Rehan may use a program without paying, and he may also read, change and share its source code. The program is best described as:
x: Being able to read and change the source code is what marks open-source software. Freeware is also free to use, but its source code is normally not given.

q: A work that is not protected by copyright, so anyone may use, copy and change it freely, is said to be in the:
x: Public domain works have no copyright owner who can restrict their use. A licence agreement is what sets the conditions for using protected software.

q: A student copies paragraphs from a website into her assignment and hands it in as her own work without naming the source. This is:
x: Plagiarism is presenting someone else's work or ideas as your own. Hacking is unauthorised access to a computer system, which has not happened here.

q: Hira wants to use a chart from a website in her school report. What is the most appropriate thing to do?
o: Credit the source and follow any conditions for its use
Copy it and remove the owner's name
Copy it, since everything online is free
Redraw it exactly and call it her own
x: Giving credit and respecting the owner's conditions is ethical and lawful use. Online content is still protected by copyright, and redrawing it as her own is plagiarism.

q: A student guesses a teacher's password, logs into the school's result system and changes his own marks. What has he done?
o: Used the system in a fair way
Only broken a rule of netiquette
Gained unauthorised access, a computer crime
Made a lawful backup of the data
x: Entering a system with someone else's password and changing data without permission is unauthorised access (hacking), a crime. It is far more serious than a lapse in online manners.

q: Someone uses another person's name, CNIC number and photos to open accounts and pretend to be that person online. This is:
x: Identity theft is stealing personal details to impersonate someone, often for fraud. Software piracy is illegal copying of software, which is not involved here.

q: A student keeps sending threatening and insulting messages to a classmate on social media. This behaviour is called:
x: Cyberbullying is using digital media to repeatedly threaten, insult or harass someone. Phishing is tricking people into revealing personal details.

q: A torch (flashlight) app asks for permission to read the user's contacts and track her location at all times. What is the main concern?
o: Copyright, as it copies the user's photos
Plagiarism, as it uses another app's name
Privacy, as it collects personal data it does not need
Piracy, as the app is free to download
x: A torch app needs no contacts or location, so collecting them is a privacy risk. Being free to download does not make an app pirated.

q: A tuition centre's online sign-up form must collect only what it needs to enrol and contact students. Which set of fields best follows this privacy practice?
o: Name, class, phone and bank card number
Name, class, phone and home Wi-Fi password
Name, phone and every social media password
x: Good privacy practice is to collect only the personal data needed for the purpose; name, class and phone are enough to enrol and contact a student. Card numbers and passwords are sensitive and not needed here.

q: When software is installed, the user is asked to accept a legal agreement stating how it may be used. This is the:
x: The licence agreement (often called the EULA) sets out the user's rights and limits, such as how many computers it may be installed on. Accepting it is a legal step, not a violation.

q: During a lab class, Usman finds that the previous student is still logged in to her e-mail on a shared computer. What is the ethical thing to do?
o: Read her messages but not reply
Log her out without reading anything
Send a joke message from her account
Change her password to teach her a lesson
x: Respecting privacy means not reading or using someone else's account; logging out protects her. Reading the messages, even without replying, still invades her privacy.

q: Which statement about copyright is correct?
o: It protects an idea even if it has never been written down
It lets anyone copy software once they have bought one copy
It protects only works that are published on paper
It protects the way an idea is expressed, not the idea itself
x: Copyright covers the expression of an idea, such as the actual text, code or recording, not the bare idea. Buying one copy does not give the right to make more copies, and digital works are protected too.

q: A student scans a paid e-book and shares the PDF with his whole class group so nobody needs to buy it. This is:
o: Fair sharing of public domain work
Legal because it is for studying
Allowed because the book was bought once
x: Copying and distributing a whole paid book without the owner's permission breaks copyright. Buying one copy gives the right to read it, not to give copies to everyone.

q: Which of the following is NOT a computer crime?
o: Buying a licensed copy of software
x: Buying a licensed copy is the lawful way to obtain software. The other three are unauthorised access, deliberate damage and theft, which are all computer crimes.

q: What is meant by the digital divide?
o: The division of a hard disk into separate parts
The gap between people who have access to computers and the Internet and those who do not
The difference between analogue and digital signals
The split of a network into LAN and WAN parts
x: The digital divide is the gap in access to and use of digital technology between groups of people. Dividing a disk is partitioning, which is unrelated.

q: Students in a city have fast Internet at home, while students in a remote village have no connection at all. This difference is an example of:
x: Unequal access to the Internet between places, such as city and village, is a classic case of the digital divide. Algorithmic bias is about unfair results from computer systems.

q: Which action would most directly help reduce the digital divide?
o: Making all websites charge a monthly fee
Selling computers only in large cities
Setting up free computer labs with Internet in rural schools
x: Giving people who lack access the devices, connection and practice they need narrows the divide. Fees and limiting sales to cities would widen it.

q: A family owns a smartphone with Internet, but no one in the family knows how to use it to fill an online admission form. What does this show about the digital divide?
o: It includes a gap in digital skills, not only in access
It no longer applies once a device is owned
It is only about the price of computers
It affects only people in large cities
x: The digital divide covers skills and knowledge as well as access; owning a device does not help if people cannot use it. Thinking it ends once a device is owned is the common mistake.

q: A face-recognition system was trained mostly on photos of light-skinned faces and makes more mistakes with darker-skinned faces. What is the main cause?
o: A virus in the camera software
Too many users at the same time
x: When training data does not represent all groups, the system learns patterns that work poorly for the missing groups; this is bias in computing. A slow connection would not make errors depend on skin colour.

q: A company trains a hiring program on its past hiring records, in which mostly men were chosen. The program now ranks male applicants higher. What is the best first step to fix this?
o: Give the program a faster processor
Check and correct the training data and test results across groups
Hide the program's results from the managers
Train it on even more of the same past records
x: The program copied bias already present in the historical data, so the data must be reviewed and the results tested for fairness across groups. More of the same records would only strengthen the bias.

q: Which practice best helps to reduce bias in a computer system that makes decisions about people?
o: Using data from only one city to keep it simple
Letting the system decide without anyone reviewing it
Keeping the training data secret from testers
Using diverse, representative data and testing it on different groups
x: Diverse data and fairness testing across groups reveal and reduce bias. Data from one place, or results that nobody reviews, let bias go unnoticed.

q: Zara shares a group project document. Two members only need to read it. Which permission should she give them?
x: Giving people only the access they need (view only) protects the document from accidental or unwanted changes. Edit rights are unnecessary for people who only read.

q: A teammate accidentally deletes a whole section of a shared online document. Which feature lets the group bring back the earlier text?
x: Version history keeps earlier saved versions of a shared document so they can be viewed and restored. Spell check and word count do not keep old content.

q: Asad receives an e-mail saying his bank account is blocked and asking him to click a link and log in. What is the safest action?
o: Do not click; contact the bank through its official website or helpline
Click the link quickly before the account closes
Reply with his account number to ask for help
Forward the e-mail to friends to warn them, then log in
x: Urgent messages with login links are a common phishing trick, so he should check through the bank's own official contact details. Clicking the link or replying with details gives the attacker what he wants.

q: Why should operating system and app updates be installed promptly?
o: They always make the screen brighter
They often fix security weaknesses that attackers could use
They delete the user's old files to free space
They turn off the need for passwords
x: Updates (patches) close security holes found in the software. Leaving software unpatched lets attackers use weaknesses that are already publicly known.

q: Which activity is riskiest to do on a free, open public Wi-Fi network at a cafe?
x: On an open network others may be able to watch traffic, so sensitive logins like banking are the biggest risk. Reading public information exposes no personal secrets.

q: The trail of posts, photos, comments and searches a person leaves online is called their:
x: A digital footprint is the record of a person's online activity, which can last a long time. The digital divide is the gap in access to technology.

q: In online messages, writing whole sentences in CAPITAL LETTERS is considered poor netiquette because it:
x: Netiquette (online manners) treats all-capital text as shouting, which is rude. It has nothing to do with storage or viruses.

q: Nida uses the same password for her e-mail, bank and social media accounts. What is the main danger?
o: Her computer will run more slowly
If one site leaks the password, all her accounts are at risk
Her accounts will be deleted after a month
She cannot log in from a different computer
x: When one password protects many accounts, a single leak or guess opens all of them. Using a different strong password for each account limits the damage.

q: Which is the most reliable source for the official date of an entrance test?
o: A message forwarded in a family chat group
An anonymous comment under a video
A screenshot posted on a social media page
The official website of the university that holds the test
x: Official sites publish information directly from the organisation responsible. Forwarded messages, comments and screenshots may be old, edited or false.

q: Which information is safest to keep private and not post publicly online?
o: The name of your favourite book
A photo of a sunset you took
Your home address and phone number
x: A home address and phone number let strangers locate or contact you, so they should stay private. The other items reveal little that could be misused.

q: A class teacher wants to share a document of students' marks with three other teachers. Which sharing setting is safest?
o: Anyone with the link can edit
Share with only those three teachers by name
Anyone with the link can view
Post the link in the class group
x: Sharing with named people keeps private marks within the people who need them. Any 'anyone with the link' setting means a forwarded link opens the document to anyone, and editing access adds the risk of changes.

q: A dramatic news message is being forwarded widely on social media. What is the responsible thing to do before sharing it?
o: Forward it at once to as many people as possible
Add more details to make it interesting
Check it against trusted news sources
Share it, since many people have already shared it
x: Verifying with reliable sources stops false information from spreading. Many people sharing a message does not make it true.

q: Kamran must leave his office computer for a few minutes while he is logged in. What is the safest thing to do?
o: Lock the screen so a password is needed
Leave it open, since he will return soon
Write his password on a note beside it
Turn off the antivirus to save power
x: Locking the screen stops others using his logged-in account while he is away. Leaving it open, even briefly, lets anyone act in his name.
